title: A Church Once Famous
sum: The church of God in Rome greets the church of God in Corinth, both living in their cities as "resident aliens" (1:0). Rome apologizes for writing late: sudden misfortunes have struck it, one after another (1:1). The subject is a "rebellion" at Corinth, stirred up by "a handful of rash and headstrong people", which has made a famous church's name a byword.

Before any rebuke the letter praises. Every visitor admired Corinth's faith, its godliness, its generous welcome of guests and its sure knowledge. The church played no favorites, walked in God's laws, submitted to its leaders and honored the older people; the young were modest, the women blameless and devoted to their homes (1:2-3).

views.H: The "misfortunes and calamities" of 1:1 are the main clue to the date. Lightfoot read them as Domitian's persecution and dated the letter about AD 95 or 96; Lake allows c. 96 if that is right, but says "we know very little about the alleged persecution in the time of Domitian" and that it is "safest" to put the letter between 75 and 110.
views.N: The greeting copies Paul's to the same church (1 Corinthians 1:2-3) and the "resident alien" language of 1 Peter (1 Peter 1:17; 1 Peter 2:11). The praise of Corinth's "knowledge" recalls Paul's thanks that they were made rich in it (1 Corinthians 1:5).
views.O: Rome writes as one church to another, with no named writer. Lightfoot points out that 1:1 speaks of "the matters of dispute" among the Corinthians, not of questions they sent to Rome: the Roman Christians, he judged, had heard of the trouble by report and wrote "unsolicited". Whether the letter shows an authority of the Roman church over other churches is taken up where the letter speaks of its own authority (59:1; 63:2).
views.G: The vocabulary is that of Greek civic speeches: stasis, "rebellion" or civil strife, against a city's honored "name"; a city with a fine reputation for hospitality. Rome addresses Corinth as one city might another.

deep.b: Lake (introduction): the letter is later than Nero's persecution (chapter 5) and regards the age of the apostles as past (42; 44), so it "can therefore scarcely be older than 75-80 A.D."; it speaks of elders appointed by the apostles who were still alive (44) and shows no trace of second-century controversies, so it is "probably not much later than 100 A.D." If chapter 1 refers to Domitian, it is about 96, but Lake warns how little is known of that persecution and concludes: "It is safest to say that it must be dated between 75 and 110 A.D.; but within these limits there is a general agreement among critics to regard as most probable the last decade of the first century." Lightfoot argued firmly for AD 95-96.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 1:2-3; 1 Peter 1:1-2; 1 Peter 2:11; Philippians 3:20; Titus 2:3-5; 1 Corinthians 1:5

settings.what: The letter as a whole
settings.by: The church of God in Rome (tradition names Clement as its writer)
settings.to: The church of God in Corinth
settings.when: Probably in the 90s (Lake: between 75 and 110), after some at Corinth had removed elders from office
settings.why: To end the revolt: to shame the rebels by the church's own past, call them to repentance and humility, and urge the church to restore its elders and keep peace.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after a few of its members had removed elders from office (44:6; 47:6). The letter was carried by messengers from Rome (63:3; 65:1) and meant to be read aloud to the whole church. It was still read there long after: Dionysius, a later overseer of Corinth, wrote to Rome that the church had read a Roman letter on the Lord's day, "as also from the former epistle, which was written to us through Clement" (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

settings.what: Greeting and praise of Corinth's past
settings.by: The church at Rome
settings.to: The whole church at Corinth, "beloved"
settings.when: At the opening of the letter, before the rebuke
settings.why: To win a hearing: by recalling what Corinth was, the church at Rome makes the present revolt look foreign to it, "alien and foreign to God's chosen" (1:1), and gives the rest of the church a self it can return to.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: Peace, Deep and Rich
sum: The praise continues. The Corinthians were humble, happier to give than to receive, content with what Christ gives for the journey, with his words in their hearts and his sufferings before their eyes. So they had "peace, deep and rich", a hunger to do good, and the Holy Spirit poured out on all (2:1-2).

They prayed for mercy even for sins they had not meant, strove day and night for all God's chosen, held no grudges, mourned their neighbors' failings as their own, and hated every rebellion and split. Their life as citizens of God's city was their adornment, and the Lord's commands were written on their hearts (2:3-8).

views.N: The chapter is woven from New Testament phrases: "Giving is more blessed than receiving" (Acts 20:35), "ready for any good work" (Titus 3:1), the heart as a tablet (2 Corinthians 3:3), the outpoured Spirit (Acts 2:17).
views.J: "The Lord's commands and rulings" and the heart's tablets are the language of Proverbs and Deuteronomy (Proverbs 3:3; Proverbs 7:3; Deuteronomy 6:6); prayer for unintended sins recalls the law of Leviticus 4.
views.G: Clement pictures the church as a well-run city: a "way of life as citizens" (politeia, 2:8), no faction (stasis), each in his place. Greek speeches on concord praised cities in just this way before calling them back to harmony.

echoes: Acts 20:35; Titus 3:1; Proverbs 7:3; 2 Corinthians 3:3; Acts 2:17; 1 Corinthians 1:10; Philippians 1:27

settings.what: The praise of the old Corinth (continued)
settings.by: The church at Rome
settings.to: The church at Corinth
settings.when: Before the rebuke of chapter 3
settings.why: Each virtue named here is the opposite of what the revolt has brought: humility against boasting, submission against rebellion, peace against splits.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: The Beloved Grew Fat and Kicked
sum: Then the turn: prosperity spoiled Corinth, and Scripture came true, "The beloved one ate and drank, and he grew broad and grew fat, and he kicked" (3:1, from the Greek Deuteronomy 32:15). Out of this came "jealousy and envy, fighting and rebellion, persecution and disorder, war and captivity" (3:2).

The dishonored rose against the honored, the senseless against the sensible, the young against the elders (3:3). Righteousness and peace are far away, because each one walks by his own evil heart and has taken up an unrighteous jealousy, the very thing through which "death came into the world" (3:4).

views.J: Two pieces of the Greek Old Testament frame the chapter: the Song of Moses, where the Septuagint calls Israel "the beloved one" (Deuteronomy 32:15), and Isaiah 3:5, where society turns upside down. The line on death is from the Wisdom of Solomon (2:24), which Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include.
views.N: Paul had already found "jealousy and strife" at Corinth (1 Corinthians 3:3), and he linked death's entry into the world with sin (Romans 5:12). Clement links it with jealousy.
views.H: "The young against the elders" is the first hint of what happened: younger or newer members moved against the church's elders (44:6; 47:6). The list of 3:2 ends in "war and captivity", words too large for a church quarrel; they are stock words of a speech on civil strife.

echoes: Deuteronomy 32:15; Isaiah 3:5; Wisdom of Solomon 2:24; Romans 5:12; 1 Corinthians 3:3; James 3:14-16

settings.what: Jealousy and envy: what they have done
settings.by: The church at Rome
settings.to: The church at Corinth
settings.when: The first main section of the argument
settings.why: To name the root of the revolt and show from Scripture and recent history where jealousy leads: murder, exile, rebellion, the deaths of apostles.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

settings.what: The beloved one who grew fat (Deuteronomy 32:15, in Greek)
settings.by: Moses, in his song; quoted by the church at Rome as "what is written"
settings.to: In Deuteronomy, the whole assembly of Israel before it entered the land (Deuteronomy 31:30)
settings.when: In the Song of Moses, sung before his death
settings.why: In Deuteronomy, to warn Israel that plenty would make it turn from God; in the letter, to tell Corinth that its honor and room to grow led to the revolt.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: From Cain to Saul
sum: Clement quotes the story of Cain and Abel from the Greek Genesis (4:1-6) and draws the moral: "jealousy and envy led to a brother's murder" (4:7). Six more examples follow in quick strokes, each beginning with jealousy: Jacob fleeing Esau, Joseph sold into slavery, Moses driven from Egypt by his own people's words, Aaron and Miriam outside the camp, Dathan and Abiram swallowed alive into Hades, and David hunted by Saul (4:8-13).

The examples are freely told. Numbers says only Miriam was shut outside the camp (Numbers 12:14-15); Genesis does not call Esau's grudge "jealousy"; but each case fits the pattern Clement wants: rivalry against a brother or against the leader God had chosen.

views.J: The Cain story is quoted from the Septuagint, whose Genesis 4:7 differs from the Hebrew ("If you made your offering rightly but did not divide it rightly...", 4:4). The rest uses the Greek Bible's words: allophyloi for the Philistines (4:13), therapōn, "attendant", for Moses (4:12).
views.N: Stephen's speech in Acts 7 runs through the same story with the same words: "Out of jealousy the patriarchs sold Joseph" (Acts 7:9) and "Who put you in charge as ruler and judge over us?" (Acts 7:27). Hebrews 11 uses Cain and Abel and Moses in its own list.
views.H: Lists of examples (Greek paradeigmata) were a standard tool of persuasion in Greek speeches and in Jewish teaching, as in Sirach 44-50, 4 Maccabees and Hebrews 11. Clement's list may draw on such a Jewish collection; nothing in it requires a source beyond the Greek Bible.

deep.title: Every example is a revolt against a brother or a leader (Claude's theory)
deep.b: Clement's seven examples are not chosen at random. Three are brothers against brothers (Cain, Esau, Joseph's brothers). Four are people turning on the leader God had set up: Moses' own countryman, Aaron and Miriam against Moses, Dathan and Abiram against "God's attendant", Saul against the anointed David. That is exactly the Corinthian situation: members of one family moving against the elders the apostles had appointed (44:2-6). Clement never says this; he lets the list say it. The overlap with published study is general (that the examples suit the situation), not this exact count.

echoes: Genesis 4:3-8; Genesis 27:41-45; Genesis 37:11; Exodus 2:14; Numbers 12:1-15; Numbers 16:1-35; Psalm 106:16-18; 1 Samuel 18:6-12; Acts 7:9; Acts 7:27-28; Hebrews 11:4

settings.what: God's words to Cain (quoted from Genesis 4)
settings.by: God, in the story; quoted by the church at Rome
settings.to: Cain
settings.when: After God accepted Abel's offering and not Cain's
settings.why: Inside the story, a warning to Cain to master his anger; in the letter, the first proof that jealousy kills.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

settings.what: The words that drove Moses out (Exodus 2:14)
settings.by: A Hebrew Moses had tried to correct
settings.to: Moses
settings.when: The day after Moses killed the Egyptian
settings.why: In Exodus, a challenge to Moses' right to judge; in the letter, a picture of God's people rejecting the leader God would send.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: Peter and Paul
sum: Clement turns from "the examples from long ago" to "the athletes closest to our own time" (5:1). Because of jealousy and envy "the greatest and most righteous pillars" were hunted down and kept up the contest until death (5:2). Peter endured many hardships and, "having borne his witness so", went to his place of glory (5:4).

Paul showed the way to the prize of endurance: seven times in chains, banished, stoned, a herald in East and West, he taught righteousness to the whole world, came to "the far limit of the West", bore his witness "before the rulers" and was taken up into the holy place (5:5-7). The New Testament does not tell the story of either death; John 21:18-19 and 2 Timothy 4:6 only look ahead to them.
readings: Clement writes in the generation after the apostles and from the city where they were remembered as dying. Read this way, the chapter is a witness that both suffered and died for their testimony, that Paul traveled beyond what Acts records (perhaps to Spain), and that their deaths were linked with the persecution of chapter 6.

Clement is not writing history but an argument against jealousy. Read this way, he chooses only what serves his point (jealousy and endurance) and says nothing of place, date or manner. Every detail beyond that, Rome, Nero, Spain, must come from other sources.

views.H: Lightfoot argued that martyrēsas, "having borne witness", means martyrdom here, though the word was not yet fixed; that "the far limit of the West" is Spain, not Rome; and that the many martyrs of 6:1 are Nero's victims. The chapter itself names no place and no emperor.
views.N: The chapter assumes much that the New Testament records (Paul's imprisonments and stoning, 2 Corinthians 11:23-25; his plan to visit Spain, Romans 15:24, 28) and adds what it does not (seven imprisonments, preaching in the West). John 21:18-19 already points to Peter's death; 2 Timothy 4:6-8 to Paul's.
views.O: The chapter says that both apostles bore their witness and went to glory, and Lightfoot takes the "among us" of 6:1, where the many martyrs are joined to "these men", to mean the Roman Christians. It does not say that either apostle founded the church at Rome or held an office there. The question of Peter's successors belongs to the Matthew 16 and Luke 22 cards.
views.G: The language is the Greek gymnasium and stadium: athletes, the contest, the prize (brabeion), the arena (7:1). Paul is a "herald", like the herald who announced the games and the winners.

deep.h: What chapter 5 says, and what it does not
deep.b:
It says: Peter and Paul suffered because of jealousy; both "bore witness" and went to a place of glory; Paul was in chains seven times, was banished and stoned, preached East and West, reached "the far limit of the West" and bore witness "before the rulers" (5:4-7). The next sentence joins to them "a great multitude of the chosen" who suffered "among us" (6:1).

It does not say: where they died, how (crucifixion, beheading), under which emperor, or whose jealousy was to blame. Lightfoot reads "among us" as Rome and the multitude as Nero's victims, and he gathers the other early witnesses (Dionysius of Corinth that the two "bore witness at the same time"). Later writers add the details: the site's Peter and Paul topics give them, with their sources.

Lightfoot shows that Greek and Latin writers used such phrases for the far west of Spain, at the Pillars of Hercules, and finds it "incredible" that a writer at Rome would call Rome "the extreme west". Paul had planned to go to Spain (Romans 15:24, 28), and the Muratorian Fragment, which Lightfoot quotes, speaks of "the departure of Paul from the city ... to Spain". Those who hold that Paul died at the end of the Roman captivity, he says, must take it as Rome itself. He lists the other readings proposed: "to his extreme limit towards the west" (Baur, Schenkel), "to the sunset of his labours" (Reuss), "to the boundary between the east and west" (Schrader, Hilgenfeld), "to the goal or centre of the west" (Matthies), and "before the supreme power of the west" (Wieseler, Schaff). If Spain is right, Paul was released after Acts 28 and traveled again before his death, as the traditional view of the Pastoral Letters also holds.

echoes: Galatians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 9:24-27; John 21:18-19; Romans 15:24; Romans 15:28; 2 Corinthians 11:23-27; Acts 14:19; 2 Timothy 4:6-8; 1 Peter 2:21

settings.what: Examples from "our own generation"
settings.by: The church at Rome
settings.to: The church at Corinth
settings.when: After the examples from Scripture
settings.why: To bring the warning home: jealousy did not only work in ancient stories; it killed the apostles the Corinthians knew by name (1 Corinthians 1:12) and many Christians at Rome.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: A Great Multitude, and the Women
sum: To Peter and Paul "a great multitude of the chosen was gathered", who suffered outrages and tortures because of jealousy and became "the finest example" among the Christians of Rome (6:1). Women too were hunted down "as Danaids and Dirces"; they suffered terrible outrages, yet reached the end of faith's race and received a noble prize, "though their bodies were weak" (6:2).

Jealousy does more: it has turned wives from husbands, undoing Adam's words over Eve, "This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh" (6:3), and it has torn down great cities and uprooted great nations (6:4).

views.H: Lightfoot connected the multitude with Nero's persecution after the fire of Rome in AD 64, comparing Tacitus's "huge multitude" (Annals 15.44), and explained "Danaids and Dirces" by Nero's taste for executions staged as scenes from myth. All the witnesses have the phrase, but Lake thinks it "perhaps corrupt".
views.G: Dirce, in Greek myth, was tied to a bull and dragged to death; the Danaids were the daughters of Danaus, punished in the underworld. Roman shows sometimes made the condemned act out such stories as they died, which is the setting Lightfoot proposed.
views.N: Hebrews speaks of Christians "put on display like a show in the theater, with insults and troubles" (Hebrews 10:33), and Revelation of a woman "drunk with the blood of the saints" (compare Revelation 17:6).

deep.b: The phrase is in every witness: Codex Alexandrinus, the Constantinople manuscript and the Latin, Syriac and Coptic versions. Read as it stands, it most likely means women who were made to play the parts of Dirce and the Danaids in the arena. Lightfoot found Dirce's story apt for such a show and the Danaids' hard to fit. Because the plural names are so awkward, Wordsworth proposed reading neanides, paidiskai, "young girls, slave girls" ("women, young girls, slave girls"), an emendation Lightfoot once printed and still favored; Tischendorf called it a "very free conjecture". Lake prints the manuscripts' text and says no satisfactory emendation is known. See the variant.

echoes: Revelation 7:9-14; Hebrews 10:32-34; 1 Corinthians 4:9; Genesis 2:23-24; 1 Peter 3:7

settings.what: Adam's words over the woman (Genesis 2:23, in Greek)
settings.by: Adam, "our father"
settings.to: The woman God had built from his rib and brought to him (Genesis 2:22)
settings.when: At the first marriage, in the garden
settings.why: In Genesis, the joy of the first union; in the letter, to show what jealousy breaks when it turns wives away from their husbands.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: The Same Arena
sum: Rome writes not only to warn Corinth but to remind itself: "We stand in the same arena, and the same contest lies ahead of us" (7:1). So let all turn from empty worries to "the rule handed down to us" and see what pleases the one who made us (7:2-3).

Look at the blood of Christ, precious to his Father: poured out for our salvation, it brought the gift of repentance to the whole world (7:4). In every generation the Master gave "a place for repentance": Noah preached it and those who listened were saved; Nineveh repented at Jonah's word and received salvation, though they were strangers to God (7:5-7).

views.N: The blood of Christ "poured out" (Matthew 26:28) and "of great worth" (1 Peter 1:19); repentance as God's gift (Acts 5:31; Acts 11:18); Noah as "a herald of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:5); Nineveh's repentance at Jonah's preaching (Matthew 12:41).
views.J: "A place for repentance" is the idiom of Wisdom of Solomon 12:10 and Hebrews 12:17. Clement's picture of Noah preaching goes beyond Genesis.
views.O: "The rule handed down to us" (7:2) is an early instance of the language of tradition. Churches that give tradition a place beside Scripture and those that hold Scripture alone as the rule both cite such passages; the topic page on Scripture and tradition gives the views.

echoes: 1 Peter 1:19; Matthew 26:28; Acts 11:18; Wisdom of Solomon 12:10; Hebrews 12:17; 2 Peter 2:5; Jonah 3:4-10; Matthew 12:41

settings.what: A call to repentance
settings.by: The church at Rome
settings.to: The church at Corinth, the rebels above all
settings.when: After the long warning about jealousy
settings.why: To open a door: the rebels can still turn back, because God has always given room to repent, even to Gentiles; Rome counts itself among those who need the warning.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: As I Live, Says the Lord
sum: The prophets, "those who served God's grace", spoke about repentance through the Holy Spirit (8:1). The Master himself swore an oath: "As I live, says the Lord, I do not want the sinner's death so much as his repentance" (8:2). He added a promise in words no Bible has: even if sins reach from earth to sky, redder than scarlet and blacker than sackcloth, if they turn back with all their heart and say "Father", he will hear them as a holy people (8:3).

"In another place" comes Isaiah 1:16-20 from the Greek: wash, stop doing evil, learn to do good; though your sins are like crimson, I will make them white as snow (8:4). So God, who wants all he loves to share in repentance, made it firm by his almighty will (8:5).

views.J: Three prophetic texts in their Greek form: Ezekiel 33:11 shortened, an unknown passage (which Clement of Alexandria quotes and ascribes to Ezekiel), and Isaiah 1:16-20, whose Greek differs from the Hebrew in several lines ("Rescue the one who is wronged"; "I will make them as white as snow").
views.H: Lightfoot suspected the unknown quotation came from a lost book under Ezekiel's name, since Clement of Alexandria quotes part of it "through Ezekiel". The site lists such a book as the Apocryphon of Ezekiel. It shows that the Roman church of Clement's day treated such a text as God's word.
views.N: The thought is that of 2 Peter 3:9, the Lord "wants all to arrive at repentance", and of the father who welcomes the son who comes back (Luke 15:20-24).

echoes: Ezekiel 33:11; Ezekiel 18:23; Ezekiel 18:30-32; Isaiah 1:16-20; Jeremiah 3:19-22; 2 Peter 3:9; Apocryphon of Ezekiel

settings.what: God's oath and promises of forgiveness
settings.by: God, through the prophets (Ezekiel, an unknown prophecy, Isaiah)
settings.to: "The house of Israel", Israel in the prophets' day
settings.when: Israel's sins in the prophets' time
settings.why: In the prophets, a call to Israel to turn back before judgment; in the letter, proof that the same God offers the Corinthian rebels forgiveness if they repent.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: Those Who Served Perfectly
sum: So let us obey God's glorious will, fall down before him begging for mercy, and leave behind useless effort, fighting and the jealousy that leads to death (9:1). Look at those who served God perfectly (9:2).

Enoch was found righteous through obedience and was taken away, "and his death was never found" (9:3). Noah was found faithful: he preached a new birth to the world, and through him the Master brought safely through the creatures that went into the ark "together in harmony" (9:4).

views.N: Enoch and Noah are the first two examples of faith after Abel in Hebrews 11:5-7. Clement's list (9-12) resembles that chapter, but his theme is obedience and hospitality rather than faith alone.
views.J: "He was not found" is the Greek of Genesis 5:24, quoted in Hebrews 11:5. Sirach 44:16-17 also praises Enoch and Noah side by side.

echoes: Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5-7; Sirach 44:16-17; Genesis 6:9; 2 Peter 2:5; Matthew 19:28

settings.what: Examples of obedience, faith and hospitality
settings.by: The church at Rome
settings.to: The church at Corinth
settings.when: After the call to repentance
settings.why: To set beside the examples of jealousy (4-6) examples of the opposite: people saved because they obeyed God and welcomed others. Each detail (the animals in harmony, Lot's wife "not in harmony") points at Corinth.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: Abraham the Friend
sum: Abraham, called "the friend", was found faithful because he obeyed God's words (10:1). He left a small land, a weak family and a little house to inherit God's promises (10:2). Clement quotes three promises from the Greek Genesis: the call to go (10:3), the land in every direction and offspring like the sand (10:4-5), and the stars, ending "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness" (10:6).
"Because of his faith and hospitality" he was given a son in old age, and because he obeyed, he offered him as a sacrifice to God on the mountain God showed him (10:7).

views.N: Genesis 15:6 is the verse Paul uses for faith apart from works (Romans 4:3) and James for faith working with works (James 2:21-23). Clement surrounds it with obedience and hospitality. He will say later that we are justified through faith, not through ourselves (32:4), and then ask whether Christians may therefore be idle from doing good (33:1): the faith and works discussion belongs to part 21-39 and the cards at Romans 3 and James 2.
views.J: The quotations follow the Septuagint: "you will be blessed" for the Hebrew "be a blessing" (Genesis 12:2), "sand" for "dust" (Genesis 13:16), "all the tribes of the earth". Abraham as God's friend is from Isaiah 41:8 and 2 Chronicles 20:7.

echoes: Genesis 12:1-3; Genesis 13:14-16; Genesis 15:5-6; Genesis 18:1-10; Genesis 22:1-14; Romans 4:3; James 2:21-23; Hebrews 11:8-19

settings.what: God's promises to Abraham (Genesis 12, 13, 15)
settings.by: God
settings.to: Abraham
settings.when: At his call, after Lot parted from him, and under the night sky
settings.why: In Genesis, to give Abraham land, offspring and blessing; in the letter, to show what obedience gains: leaving little, Abraham inherited much.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: Lot and His Wife
sum: When the whole region was judged by fire and sulfur, Lot was saved out of Sodom "because of his hospitality and godliness", and the Master showed that he does not abandon those who hope in him (11:1).

Lot's wife went out with him but "thought differently and was not in harmony with him"; she became a pillar of salt "to this day", a sign that the double-minded and those who doubt God's power bring judgment on themselves (11:2).

views.N: 2 Peter calls Lot "righteous" (2 Peter 2:7-8); Jesus says "Remember Lot's wife!" (Luke 17:32). "Double-minded" is the word of James 1:8.
views.J: The Wisdom of Solomon calls the pillar of salt "the monument of a soul that would not believe" (Wisdom of Solomon 10:7). Clement reads the story through hospitality (Genesis 19:1-3) and harmony.

echoes: Genesis 19:1-29; Genesis 19:26; 2 Peter 2:6-9; Luke 17:28-32; Wisdom of Solomon 10:6-7; James 1:8

title: Rahab and the Scarlet Sign
sum: "Because of her faith and hospitality Rahab the prostitute was saved" (12:1). Clement retells Joshua 2: the spies sent to Jericho, the king's men at her door, her answer that the men had gone, her confession that "the Lord God is giving this land into your hands", and the spies' promise to save all under her roof (12:2-6).

The sign they gave her, something scarlet hung from her house, made it plain "that through the blood of the Lord there will be redemption for all who believe and hope in God" (12:7). So the woman had "not only faith but prophecy" (12:8).
readings: Read as a story of faith

Rahab is a Gentile and a prostitute who believed what she had heard of Israel's God and acted on it at the risk of her life. Read this way, the chapter is about faith and welcome, like Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25.
Read as a figure of Christ

The scarlet cord is a sign of Christ's blood, and Rahab a prophet without words. Read this way, Clement stands at the start of a long Christian tradition (Justin, Irenaeus, Origen) of finding Christ in the Old Testament's objects and events.

views.N: Hebrews 11:31 praises Rahab's faith; James 2:25 her works; Matthew 1:5 places her among Jesus' ancestors. Clement's "faith and hospitality" holds Hebrews and James together.
views.J: Jewish tradition remembers Rahab with honor; the site's Joshua 2 notes give the Jewish readings. Clement's retelling follows the story closely but not word for word, and the scarlet cord is, in Joshua, the agreed sign (Joshua 2:18-21).
views.H: Lightfoot traces the reading of the scarlet cord as Christ's blood from here to Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho 111, Irenaeus and Origen, and suggests Hebrews 9:19 may have prompted it. Codex Alexandrinus and Clement of Alexandria read "Rahab the prostitute"; the other witnesses soften it (see the variant).

echoes: Joshua 2:1-21; Joshua 6:22-25; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25; Matthew 1:5; Hebrews 9:19

settings.what: Rahab and the spies
settings.by: The king's men, Rahab, the spies (retold from Joshua 2)
settings.to: Each other, in Rahab's house at Jericho
settings.when: The night before Israel crossed the Jordan
settings.why: Inside the story, a bargain for her family's lives; in the letter, an example of faith shown in welcome, and of a sign that pointed to Christ.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: Be Humble
sum: So let us be humble and put away bragging, conceit, foolishness and anger, and do what is written: the wise must not boast in wisdom, the strong in strength, the rich in riches, but "let the one who boasts boast in the Lord" (13:1). Above all, keep in mind the words the Lord Jesus spoke when teaching forbearance and patience (13:1).

Seven sayings follow: show mercy, forgive, as you do, as you give, as you judge, as you show kindness, so it will be to you, and "The measure you use is the one that will be used to measure out to you" (13:2). By these let us walk humbly, for the holy word says God looks on "the one who is gentle and quiet and trembles at my sayings" (13:3-4).

views.N: The sayings stand close to the Sermon on the Mount and on the Plain (Matthew 5:7; Matthew 6:14; Matthew 7:1-2, 12; Luke 6:31, 36-38) but match neither Gospel in order or wording. Lightfoot thought Clement quoted the Gospels loosely, so that "the hypothesis ... that Clement derived the saying from oral tradition or from some lost Gospel, is not needed". The formula "the words of the Lord Jesus" is that of Acts 20:35.
views.J: The opening quotation joins Jeremiah 9:23-24 with the Greek of Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:10), which adds the same lines; Isaiah 66:2 is quoted with "gentle" for "lowly".
views.H: How Clement knew these sayings matters for how the Gospel tradition was passed on. Polycarp to the Philippians 2:3 gives a similar set, which Lightfoot thought was taken from Clement.

echoes: Jeremiah 9:23-24; 1 Samuel 2:10; 1 Corinthians 1:31; Matthew 5:7; Matthew 7:1-2; Matthew 7:12; Luke 6:31-38; Isaiah 66:2; Acts 20:35

settings.what: A call to humility
settings.by: The church at Rome
settings.to: The church at Corinth, and its rebels
settings.when: After the examples of obedience
settings.why: The rebels exalted themselves over the elders; the cure is humility, taught by Jesus' words, by Christ's own coming, and by the great humble saints.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

settings.what: Words of the Lord Jesus
settings.by: The Lord Jesus, as the church at Rome remembered his teaching
settings.to: His followers (in the Gospels, the disciples and the crowds, Matthew 5:1-2; Luke 6:17-20)
settings.when: When he was "teaching forbearance and patience"
settings.why: In Jesus' teaching, to show that God treats us as we treat others; in the letter, to call quarreling Christians to mercy and forgiveness.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

settings.what: Whom God looks on (Isaiah 66:2, in Clement's form)
settings.by: God, through Isaiah ("the holy word says")
settings.to: In Isaiah, Israel, told that heaven is God's throne and no house built for him can hold him (Isaiah 66:1-2)
settings.when: After the words of the Lord Jesus, as further proof
settings.why: In Isaiah, God prefers the humble who tremble at his word to the grandest house; in the letter, to show that God regards the gentle and quiet, not the boastful leaders of the revolt.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: Obey God, Not the Ringleaders
sum: It is right to obey God rather than follow those who, bragging and disorderly, are the leaders of a foul jealousy (14:1). To hand ourselves over to people who hurl themselves into fighting and rebellions is a great danger (14:2). Let us rather be kind to each other, as the one who made us is kind (14:3).

For Scripture says the kind will live in the land and lawbreakers will be destroyed from it (14:4, Proverbs 2:21-22 joined with Psalm 37 in Greek), and the ungodly man who towered like the cedars of Lebanon was gone when the psalmist passed by: "the man of peace has a remnant left to him" (14:5, Psalm 37:35-37 in Greek).

views.N: "Obey God rather than" echoes Acts 4:19 and Acts 5:29, where the apostles defy the Temple rulers. Clement turns the principle against the leaders of a church faction, whom he calls archēgoi, "ringleaders".
views.J: Lake's margin gives Proverbs 2:21-22 and Psalm 37:9 and 38 for 14:4, and Clement joins them: "the kind" (chrēstoi) for "the upright", picking up the call "Let us show kindness" (chrēsteusōmetha, 14:3), and the Greek Psalm's "will be destroyed" for the Greek Proverbs' "will be driven out". Psalm 37:35-37 in 14:5 follows the Septuagint, which differs from the Hebrew.

echoes: Acts 4:19; Acts 5:29; Proverbs 2:21-22; Psalm 37:9; Psalm 37:38; Psalm 37:35-37; Matthew 5:5; Hebrews 13:17

settings.what: Who keeps the land (Proverbs 2:21-22 and Psalm 37, in Greek)
settings.by: Scripture: the teacher of Proverbs, and David in Psalm 37
settings.to: In Proverbs, a son taught by his father (Proverbs 2:1); in the Psalm, the faithful tempted to envy those who do wrong (Psalm 37:1)
settings.when: After the call to be kind to each other (14:3)
settings.why: In Proverbs and the Psalm, to promise that the upright will stay and the wicked will go; in the letter, to warn that the rebels, not the kind and peaceful, will be the ones removed.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: Peace, Not Pretense
sum: Hold fast to those who keep the peace out of godliness, not to those who want peace only as a pretense (15:1). Then a chain of Scripture on lips that say one thing while the heart says another: "This people gives me honor with their lips, but their heart is far away from me" (15:2); they bless with the mouth and curse in the heart (15:3); they loved God with their mouth and lied to him with their tongue (15:4).

Let lying lips be struck dumb; may the Lord destroy the boastful tongue of those who say, "Our lips are our own. Who is lord over us?" Because of the misery of the poor the Lord will rise up and set them in safety (15:5-7).

views.N: The first quotation has the short form of Isaiah 29:13 that Jesus uses in Mark 7:6 and Matthew 15:8, not the longer form of the Greek Isaiah.
views.J: Five texts strung on one theme, mouth against heart: Isaiah 29:13, Psalm 62:4, Psalm 78:36-37, Psalm 31:18 and Psalm 12:3-5, all in their Greek form. The joining is by catchword ("lips", "mouth", "heart").
views.H: In 15:5 all the witnesses but the Syriac skip a line, from one "lying lips" to the next; Lake prints the Syriac's fuller text, which Lightfoot had restored by conjecture before the Syriac was known.

echoes: Isaiah 29:13; Mark 7:6; Matthew 15:8; Psalm 62:4; Psalm 78:36-37; Psalm 31:18; Psalm 12:3-5; Jeremiah 6:14

settings.what: Lips against heart (Isaiah 29:13; Psalms 62, 78, 31 and 12)
settings.by: God through Isaiah, and the psalmists; in 15:6-7 the Lord himself speaks (Psalm 12:5)
settings.to: In Isaiah, a people who honored God with their lips only; in the Psalms, Israel and the psalmists' hearers; in 15:6-7, the poor and the needy, for whom the Lord rises up
settings.when: After the call to hold fast to those who keep the peace out of godliness (15:1)
settings.why: To show from Scripture that words of peace without a true heart are lies, and that the Lord will silence the proud who say "Who is lord over us?" and rise up for those they crush.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: Christ the Humble One
sum: "Christ belongs to the humble, not to those who lift themselves up over his flock" (16:1). The Lord Jesus Christ, "the scepter of God's majesty", did not come with pomp, though he could have, but humble, as the Holy Spirit had spoken (16:2). Then the whole of Isaiah 53 from the Greek: the servant with no form or beauty, who carries our sins, is wounded for our lawless deeds, is led like a sheep to slaughter, is counted among the lawless and bears the sins of many (16:3-14).

Psalm 22 follows as Christ's own words: "But I am a worm and not a man" (16:15-16). The lesson: "If the Lord was so humble, what should we do, who have come under the yoke of his grace through him?" (16:17).
readings: Clement, like the New Testament (Acts 8:32-35; 1 Peter 2:21-25), reads Isaiah 53 as the Spirit speaking beforehand about Jesus. The Psalm too is Christ speaking. This is the reading of the churches.

Jewish interpreters have read the servant of Isaiah 53 as Israel, or a prophet, or the Messiah; the site's Isaiah 53 notes and the servant topic give the readings. Clement does not argue the point; he assumes the Christian reading and uses it for one virtue, humility.

views.J: Clement quotes the whole song, almost exactly as the Septuagint has it. Where the Greek differs from the Hebrew, Clement follows the Greek: "as of a little child" (16:3, from Isaiah 53:2), "carries our sins" (16:4, from Isaiah 53:4), "the Lord handed him over" (16:7, from Isaiah 53:6), "the Lord wants to cleanse him of his wound" (16:10, from Isaiah 53:10).
views.N: The New Testament quotes pieces of the same Greek song: Acts 8:32-33, 1 Peter 2:22-24, Luke 22:37, Matthew 8:17 (from the Hebrew sense), John 12:38, Romans 10:16. Clement shows a church that knew the whole song as a passion text. Philippians 2:6-8 lies behind "though he could have".
views.O: "His flock" (16:1) prepares the defense of the elders: the flock is Christ's, and those who lift themselves over it, the rebels, not the elders, are acting against him (44:3; 54:2; 57:2).

deep.h: Isaiah 53 in Clement's Greek and the site's Hebrew-based wording
deep.b:
The Plain English Translation uses the site's Isaiah wording where the Greek says the same thing, and the wording of Acts 8:32-33 and 1 Peter 2:22-24 where they quote the same Greek. The main differences:

  • 53:1 Greek adds "Lord," at the start.
  • 53:2 "We made our report before him, as of a little child": Hebrew "He came up before him like a little shoot".
  • 53:3 "who knew how to bear weakness": Hebrew "who knew sickness well".
  • 53:4 "carries our sins and suffers pain for us": Hebrew "it was our sicknesses that he carried".
  • 53:6 "the Lord handed him over for our sins": Hebrew "the LORD made the guilt of us all fall on him".
  • 53:8 "Because of the lawless deeds of my people he has come to death": Hebrew "because my people rebelled, the blow fell on him".
  • 53:9 "I will give the wicked in return for his burial": Hebrew "They gave him a burial place among the wicked".
  • 53:10 "the Lord wants to cleanse him of his wound. If you make an offering for sin": Hebrew "the LORD desired to crush him ... If his life is made a guilt offering".
  • 53:12 "because of their sins he was handed over": Hebrew "he will step in for the rebels".

Swete's Septuagint, which prints mainly Codex Vaticanus, has "our soul" in 53:10 where Clement has "your soul".

echoes: Isaiah 53:1-12; Psalm 22:6-8; Acts 8:32-35; 1 Peter 2:21-25; Luke 22:37; Matthew 27:39-43; Philippians 2:5-8; Matthew 11:29-30

settings.what: The song of the suffering servant (Isaiah 53)
settings.by: The Holy Spirit, through Isaiah, "about him", as Clement says
settings.to: In Isaiah, Israel; quoted to the church at Corinth
settings.when: Isaiah's prophecy, heard by Clement as spoken beforehand about Christ
settings.why: In the letter, to prove that Christ came humble, so that no Christian may exalt himself over the flock.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

settings.what: Psalm 22, as Christ's own words
settings.by: Christ, speaking in the Psalm ("he himself says")
settings.to: God, in the Psalm
settings.when: The sufferer mocked by the crowd; for Christians, the cross (Matthew 27:39-43)
settings.why: To show the depth of Christ's humiliation, the model for the church.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: The Humble Saints of Old
sum: Imitate the prophets who went around in goat hides and sheepskins proclaiming Christ's coming, Elijah, Elisha and Ezekiel, and all who were given a good witness (17:1). Abraham, God's friend, looking at God's glory, said "But I am earth and ashes" (17:2). Job, "righteous and blameless", still accused himself: "No one is clean of filth, not even if he lives for only one day" (17:3-4).

Moses, "faithful in all his house", through whose service God judged Egypt, did not talk big; at the bush he said, "Who am I, that you send me? But I am weak of voice and slow of tongue", and again, "But I am steam from a pot" (17:5-6), words found in no known book.

views.N: The goatskins and sheepskins are the words of Hebrews 11:37, and "faithful in all his house" is the comparison of Hebrews 3:2-5. These are among the clearest links between 1 Clement and Hebrews; part 21-39 takes up the question of dependence at chapter 36.
views.J: Each quotation is from the Greek: Genesis 18:27 ("earth and ashes" for Hebrew "dust and ashes"), Job 1:1 and 14:4-5, Exodus 3:11 and 4:10 ("weak of voice" for Hebrew "heavy of mouth"). "Steam from a pot" is unknown; Lightfoot mentions Hilgenfeld's guess, the Assumption of Moses.
views.G: "Steam from a pot", the image of a life as vapor, is common in Stoic writers, as Lightfoot notes (Seneca; Marcus Aurelius).

echoes: Hebrews 11:37; 1 Kings 19:13; 1 Kings 19:19; 2 Kings 2:13-14; Genesis 18:27; Job 1:1; Job 14:4-5; Numbers 12:7; Hebrews 3:2-5; Exodus 3:11; Exodus 4:10; James 4:14

settings.what: Humble words of Abraham, Job and Moses
settings.by: Abraham, Job and Moses, as Scripture (and one unknown writing) records them
settings.to: God (Abraham, Moses at the bush) or his hearers (Job)
settings.when: Abraham pleading for Sodom; Job in his suffering; Moses at the bush
settings.why: In the letter, to show that the greatest saints spoke of themselves lowly, while the rebels at Corinth boast.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: David's Prayer
sum: What of David, "given a good witness"? God said of him, "I have found a man to suit my heart, David son of Jesse. With eternal mercy I have anointed him" (18:1). Yet David too confessed his sin, and Clement quotes the whole of Psalm 51 from the Greek (18:2-17).

"Have mercy on me, O God ... Wash me again and again of my lawlessness ... Against you alone I sinned ... Create a pure heart in me, O God ... A broken spirit is the sacrifice for God." The point is in the frame: if the man God chose confessed like this, the Corinthian rebels can confess too.

views.J: The quotation is almost word for word the Septuagint of Psalm 50 (Psalm 51 in English). It uses "mercy" where the Hebrew has hesed ("loyal love" on the site), "lawless deed" for "rebellions", and "a governing spirit" (pneuma hēgemonikon) for the Hebrew "a generous spirit". The joined quotation in 18:1 matches Paul's in Acts 13:22.
views.N: Paul quotes the Greek of Psalm 51:4 in Romans 3:4, and the site's Romans wording is used here (18:4). Psalm 51 became the church's great psalm of repentance.
views.G: "A governing spirit" would sound to a Greek ear like the Stoic hēgemonikon, the ruling center of the self (Lightfoot).

echoes: Psalm 89:20; 1 Samuel 13:14; Acts 13:22; Psalm 51:1-17; 2 Samuel 12:1-13; Romans 3:4

settings.what: David's prayer of repentance (Psalm 51)
settings.by: David
settings.to: God
settings.when: In the Psalm's heading, after Nathan confronted him about Bathsheba (Clement does not quote the heading)
settings.why: In the Psalm, a plea for cleansing; in the letter, a model of the confession the rebels should make (compare 51:1-3).
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: The Goal of Peace
sum: The humility and submission of so many great people, "given a good witness", have made better both us and the generations before us who received God's sayings in fear and truth (19:1).

Now the letter states its goal: "let us run back to the goal of peace that was handed down to us from the beginning", look steadily at "the Father and Maker of the whole world", and hold fast to his gifts of peace (19:2). Look at him with the eyes of the soul and see how patient and free of anger he is toward all he has made (19:3).

views.G: "Father and Maker" recalls Plato's "maker and father of this universe" (Timaeus 28c), and "free of anger" is a quality Greek thinkers gave the divine. Clement speaks a language his Greek hearers knew, about the God of Genesis.
views.N: Peace as a goal "handed down" matches the New Testament's calls to keep "the unity that the Spirit gives, with peace as the tie that binds you" (Ephesians 4:3) and to "Go after peace with everyone" (Hebrews 12:14).
views.H: The chapter is a hinge. The examples (3-18) end; the picture of creation at peace (20) begins; the argument for order in the church comes later (37-44). Peace and harmony are the words that hold the letter together.

echoes: Ephesians 4:3; Hebrews 12:14; Hebrews 12:1; Philippians 3:14; Exodus 34:6; Malachi 2:10; 1 Corinthians 8:6

settings.what: The peace of creation
settings.by: The church at Rome
settings.to: The church at Corinth
settings.when: After the examples of humility; the end of the letter's first movement
settings.why: To show that peace and harmony are the order God built into the world, so that a church in revolt is out of step with all creation.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).

title: The World in Harmony
sum: A hymn to creation in order. The heavens submit to God in peace; day and night keep their course; sun, moon and the dancing choirs of stars move in harmony; the earth bears its crops in season and never quarrels with his decrees; the deeps and the world below are held by the same commands (20:1-5). The sea stays within its bars, for God said, "Up to here you will come"; the ocean and "the worlds beyond it" are steered by the same orders (20:6-8).

The seasons hand over to one another in peace; the winds do their service; springs never fail; even the smallest creatures meet in harmony and peace (20:9-10). The great Creator and Master ordered all these to be in peace and harmony, and does good to all, but most of all to us who have fled to his compassion through Jesus Christ. To him be the glory and the majesty forever (20:11-12).
readings: The chapter is a prose psalm in the line of Psalm 104, Psalm 148 and God's speech in Job 38, which Clement quotes (20:7). Creation obeys its Maker; so should his people.

The chapter is also a Greek picture of the kosmos, the ordered whole held together by concord. Clement uses that picture, but his cosmos has a Master and a Creator who does good "through our Lord Jesus Christ".

views.G: Words like homonoia (harmony), diatagē (ordering) and the stars' "choirs" belong to the Greek vocabulary of an ordered cosmos. "The worlds beyond" the ocean reflect Greek speculation about lands past the Atlantic; Lightfoot traces how Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria and Origen accepted them and later writers rejected them.
views.J: Behind the chapter stand Genesis 1 (the waters gathered into their gatherings), Job 38:8-11, Psalm 104 and Jeremiah 5:22. Job 38:11 is quoted from the Greek.
views.H: Lake prints an emendation in 20:5, "regions" for the manuscripts' "decrees", and in 20:8 follows the manuscripts' "endless" ocean where Origen and the Syriac have "impassable" (see the variants).

deep.b: Clement moves from top to bottom and back to the living: heavens (20:1), day and night (20:2), sun, moon and stars (20:3), earth and its food (20:4), the deeps and the underworld (20:5), the sea (20:6-7), the ocean and the worlds beyond (20:8), the seasons (20:9), winds, springs and the smallest animals (20:10), then the Creator and the church (20:11) and a doxology (20:12). The key words recur: "peace" (20:1, 9, 10, 11), "harmony" (20:3, 10, 11), and the commands, orders and decrees that each part keeps (20:2-8). The lesson is never stated in the chapter, but it is the letter's: everything God made keeps its place in peace.

echoes: Genesis 1:9-10; Job 38:8-11; Psalm 104:1-30; Psalm 148:1-12; Jeremiah 5:22; Jeremiah 31:35-36; Hebrews 6:18; Romans 11:36

settings.what: God's word to the sea (Job 38:11)
settings.by: God, speaking to Job out of the storm
settings.to: The sea, in God's speech; heard by Job
settings.when: God's answer to Job
settings.why: In Job, to show God's power over the chaos he bounds; in the letter, an example of creation keeping the limits God set.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, as for the whole letter (1:0-65:2).
